fields.title: What to measure in the product, not in the lab
fields.keyTakeaway: Evals catch regressions, product metrics show value, and implicit signals like question rewriting are more informative than explicit feedback.
fields.sections/0/blocks/0/text: Evals are green, users are unhappy. How is that possible?
fields.sections/1/blocks/0/text: Evals measure what we decided to measure. The gap between them and real experience is common, and without product metrics it remains invisible.
fields.sections/2/blocks/0/text: Two levels of measurement, and both are needed.
fields.sections/2/blocks/1/text: **Offline — evals.** Fast, cheap, reproducible. Catches regressions. Does not reflect real usage.
fields.sections/2/blocks/2/text: **Online — product metrics.** Slow, noisy, reflects the truth.
fields.sections/2/blocks/4/text: *Usage.* The share of users who tried the feature and the share who returned. Retention is the strongest signal of usefulness. *Completion.* The share of requests brought to a result versus drop-offs. *Explicit feedback.* "Useful" and "inaccurate" ratings. Low volume, but high quality. *Implicit signals.* Rewriting a question right after an answer is a sign of failure. Leaving the feature without action. Repeating the same question. *Impact on goals.* Conversion, average order value, support tickets.
fields.sections/2/blocks/5/text: The last one is most important and most frequently unmeasured: **an AI feature must move a product metric, not just work.**
fields.sections/2/blocks/6/text: Typical causes of the gap between evals and reality:
fields.sections/2/blocks/7/text: *The eval set does not reflect real requests.* Created by the team rather than gathered from logs. *Measuring the wrong thing.* The answer is factually correct but useless. *The problem is not the answer.* Slow, unclear, feature not found.
fields.sections/3/blocks/0/text: Online metrics for the "ask about a product" feature:
fields.sections/3/blocks/1/rows/0/0: Share of users who tried it
fields.sections/3/blocks/2/text: Rewriting in 9% of cases was a metric absent from evals that turned out more useful than ratings: people rarely click "inaccurate", but willingly re-ask.
fields.sections/3/blocks/3/text: Analyzing rewrites yielded the quarter's main conclusion: half of them were questions where the answer was correct, but too generic. Evals missed this because the criterion was "fact is correct", not "answer is useful".
fields.sections/3/blocks/4/text: We added a "specificity" criterion and replenished the set with 40 examples from rewrites. The share of rewrites dropped to 5%.
fields.sections/4/blocks/0/text: Online metrics are noisy and lag behind. Prompt decisions are made using evals, product decisions using online data.
fields.sections/5/blocks/0/text: Evals catch regressions, product metrics show value, and implicit signals like question rewriting are more informative than explicit feedback.
